title: Should You Refrigerate Potatoes?

seo.title: Should You Refrigerate Potatoes?
seo.meta_description: U.S. extension guidance generally favors cool, dark storage rather than a normal refrigerator because cold can sweeten potatoes. Recent UK evidence adds nuance.
seo.search_intent: Decide whether raw potatoes belong in the refrigerator and understand cold sweetening and acrylamide concerns.

excerpt: Most U.S. extension guidance still recommends a cool, dark, ventilated place rather than a standard refrigerator because cold storage can convert starch to sugars and make potatoes taste sweeter and brown faster. A recent UK review, however, found that home refrigeration did not materially increase acrylamide-forming potential compared with a cool dark place.
content_html:
For years, household advice sounded absolute: never put raw potatoes in the refrigerator. The underlying chemistry is real, but the practical safety question is more nuanced than the old rule suggests.

Why U.S. extension sources usually recommend cool pantry storage

Several U.S. university extension services advise storing potatoes in a cool, dark, well-ventilated location rather than a standard refrigerator. At low temperatures, potatoes can undergo cold sweetening: some starch is converted to reducing sugars.

That can make the potatoes taste sweeter and brown more quickly during frying or roasting. When reducing sugars react with the amino acid asparagine at high cooking temperatures, more acrylamide can form.

The UK Food Standards Agency recently changed its household advice

The FSA previously advised consumers not to refrigerate raw potatoes for the same cold-sweetening reason. After reviewing newer research, it now says that home refrigerator storage does not materially increase acrylamide-forming potential compared with storing potatoes in a cool, dark place.

The agency therefore allows either method at home, especially when refrigeration helps prevent food waste. That is an important update because it separates a plausible chemical mechanism from the actual size of the effect under household conditions.

So what is the practical U.S. choice?

If you have a reliably cool, dark, ventilated pantry or basement area, it remains an excellent option and avoids changes in sweetness and frying color. Typical U.S. extension recommendations for longer storage are often around 40–50°F—cooler than most homes but somewhat warmer than many refrigerators.

If your kitchen is hot and potatoes are sprouting or rotting before you use them, refrigeration can be a reasonable waste-reduction choice. Be aware that refrigerated potatoes may cook darker, especially when fried hard.

Storage is more than temperature

Keep potatoes away from light to limit greening, avoid sealed damp bags, provide airflow, and remove rotting tubers. Those factors matter whether the potatoes are in a pantry, cellar, or refrigerator.

Cooking color still matters

For fried, roasted, or baked potatoes, avoid pushing them to very dark brown. Acrylamide formation rises with high-temperature browning, so a golden color is a better target than a deeply browned surface.

Bottom line: a cool dark pantry remains the traditional U.S. default, but refrigerator storage should not be described as automatically dangerous; newer UK evidence shows the household acrylamide effect is smaller than older advice implied.

faq.question: Does refrigeration make potatoes toxic?
faq.answer: No. Cold can increase reducing sugars and change cooking color, but refrigeration does not make potatoes inherently toxic.

faq.question: Why do many U.S. extension services say not to refrigerate them?
faq.answer: Because a normal refrigerator can promote cold sweetening, which changes flavor and can increase browning during high-heat cooking.

faq.question: Why did the UK FSA change its advice?
faq.answer: It reviewed newer evidence showing that home refrigeration did not materially increase acrylamide-forming potential compared with a cool, dark place.
